 1                                                 INTRODUCTION

 2           The Defendants seek to take advantage of their dishonesty and failure to differentiate

 3   between the individual running the operation and three entities he created as a basis to dismiss the

 4   Complaint. Defendant Liévano created pseudonymous accounts to operate a deceptive and

 5   misleading advertising scheme on Facebook and Instagram, whereby the Defendants accepted

 6   payment for purportedly high-quality products but sent customers lesser quality and counterfeit

 7   products or no product at all and they also charged unauthorized recurring subscription fees. As

 8   part of the scheme, Defendant Liévano orchestrated submissions of false financial information by

 9   Judang Team LLC, Jot & Journeys (“J&J”), and Perfeos LLC (collectively, the “Entity

10   Defendants”), which evidences the intermingled financials of the three purportedly distinct

11   entities. The Defendants obtained over $8.1 million in credits to purchase advertisements that the

12   Defendants placed but never paid for.

13           By their individual conduct, each of the Defendants breached its contracts with Meta in

14   numerous ways: using Meta’s services to sell fraudulent services (bait-and-switch schemes,

15   misleading ads, inferior or nonexistent products, unauthorized recurring subscription fees,

16   concealing the true nature of the business) and collectively taking out over $8.1 million in ads

17   using credit that the Defendants have not paid for. Moreover, after Meta caught onto the scheme

18   and terminated their accounts, they created new accounts to bypass Meta’s and Instagram’s Terms

19   and Policies.

20           In addition, the Defendants committed fraud by submitting false statements and

21   withholding material, accurate information from Meta to obtain credit to place ads on Facebook

22   and Instagram.

23           The Defendants’ arguments amount to complaints about the fact that all four Defendants

24   have engaged in the same conduct. But this is not a basis to dismiss the Complaint. 1

25

26

27
     1
28    If the Court were to find any merit to any of the Defendants’ arguments, Meta respectfully seeks leave to amend the
     Complaint.
                                        2
         PLAINTIFF’S RESPONSE TO DEFENDANTS’ MOTION TO DISMISS COMPLAINT
             Case 3:25-cv-05156-TSH            Document 38         Filed 11/20/25       Page 3 of 15




 1                                  APPLICABLE LEGAL STANDARD

 2           To survive a motion to dismiss, a complaint must allege sufficient facts to state a claim for

 3   relief that is plausible on its face. The Complaint here easily meets this standard.

 4           Rule 8 requires a complaint to contain “a short and plain statement of the claim showing

 5   that the pleader is entitled to relief” such that each defendant is put on notice of the claims they

 6   must defend against. Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(a)(2); Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 555 (2007).

 7   This pleading standard does not require “detailed factual allegations” but requires sufficient facts

 8   that, when accepted as true, “state a claim for relief that is plausible on its face.” Ashcroft v. Iqbal,

 9   556 U.S. 662, 677-79 (2009) (quoting Twombly, 550 U.S. at 555, 570). On a motion to dismiss,

10   the court accepts plaintiff’s factual allegations as pled and construes all factual inferences in the

11   light most favorable to the plaintiff. Id.

12           Rule 9 lays out a heightened pleading standard for fraud-based claims, which requires

13   plaintiffs to allege “with particularity the circumstances constituting fraud.” Fed. R. Civ. P. 9(b);

14   Doe v. Roblox Corp., 602 F. Supp. 3d 1243, 1254 (N.D. Cal. 2022). Allegations of fraud “must be

15   accompanied by the who, what, when, where, and how of the misconduct charged.” Id. (citing

16   Vess v. Ciba-Geigy Corp. USA, 317 F.3d 1097, 1106 (9th Cir. 2003)).

17           In addition, “a plaintiff may plead claims against multiple defendants by referring to them

18   collectively . . . . These collective allegations are construed as applying to each defendant

19   individually.” Sprint Sols., Inc. v. Fils-Amie, 44 F. Supp. 3d 1224, 1227 (S.D. Fla. 2014) (citation

20   omitted); see also Tivoli LLC v. Sankey SPA, No. SA CV 14-1285-DOC (JCGx), 2015 WL

21   12683801, at *3-5 (C.D. Cal. Feb. 3, 2015) (“Group pleading is not fatal to a complaint if the

22   complaint still gives defendants fair notice of the claims against them.”).

23                                                ARGUMENT

24           1. Liévano Is Individually Bound to the Contracts and Is Liable for Breaching Them

25               a. Liévano Breached Meta’s Terms in His Personal Capacity

26           The Defendants argue that, because Liévano engaged in “corporate acts” and there is no

27   privity between Liévano and the corporate entities he runs and operates, the Complaint “fails to

28   plausibly allege that Liévano personally entered into or was bound by any of the cited agreements
                                        3
         PLAINTIFF’S RESPONSE TO DEFENDANTS’ MOTION TO DISMISS COMPLAINT
             Case 3:25-cv-05156-TSH            Document 38      Filed 11/20/25       Page 4 of 15




 1   (e.g., Meta’s Terms of Service, Instagram’s Terms, Meta’s Commercial Terms, Self-Serve Ad

 2   Terms, or Online Invoicing Terms).” Mot. to Dismiss at 4. This argument is incorrect. The

 3   Complaint squarely alleges that Liévano, individually, was bound by each of the contracts at issue.

 4          The first paragraph of the complaint defines Liévano in two ways: individually as

 5   “Liévano” and collectively within the defined term “Defendants.” Compl. ¶ 1. Consequently, each

 6   time the Complaint mentions either Liévano or Defendants, the allegations pertain to Defendant

 7   Liévano. The Complaint levies numerous specific allegations against Liévano that are sufficient

 8   to withstand a motion to dismiss:

 9         Liévano personally created and operated multiple Facebook and Instagram accounts and

10          thereby had notice of and agreed to Meta’s and Instagram’s Terms and Policies. Compl.

11          ¶¶ 46-48 (detailing the usernames and creation dates of multiple Facebook and Instagram

12          accounts that Liévano created and managed personally, both before and after Meta sent

13          him a cease-and-desist letter).

14         Liévano, as one of the Defendants, personally “created, controlled, and used multiple

15          Facebook and Instagram accounts, advertising accounts, and Facebook Pages, and thereby

16          received notice of, agreed to, and [was] bound by Meta’s and Instagram’s Terms and

17          Policies.” Compl. ¶ 76; see also id. ¶¶ 3, 78-82 (defining Meta’s and Instagram’s Terms

18          and Policies, which are the set of contracts at issue in the breach of contract claim).

19         Liévano personally received Meta’s February 2025 cease-and-desist letter that outlined the

20          ways in which the Defendants, including Liévano, were violating those Terms. Compl.

21          ¶¶ 72-73 & Ex. 4.

22         Liévano personally created multiple accounts after Meta disabled his accounts for violating

23          Meta’s or Instagram’s Terms and Policies. Compl. ¶ 49; see also id. ¶ 82.

24         Liévano, as one of the Defendants, personally breached Meta’s and Instagram’s Terms and

25          Policies. Compl. ¶¶ 78-82.

26   The foregoing allegations clearly describe Liévano’s personal agreement to Meta’s and

27   Instagram’s Terms and Policies and are more than sufficient to survive a motion to dismiss. See

28   Williams v. Apple, Inc., 449 F. Supp. 3d 892 (N.D. Cal. 2020) (denying a motion to dismiss upon
                                       4
        PLAINTIFF’S RESPONSE TO DEFENDANTS’ MOTION TO DISMISS COMPLAINT
               Case 3:25-cv-05156-TSH          Document 38        Filed 11/20/25      Page 5 of 15




 1   finding that plaintiffs had sufficiently alleged the existence of a contract even where they failed to

 2   allege the specific version of the contract and when they signed the contract). As an additional

 3   basis for Liévano’s personal liability, the Complaint alleges that he is the principal and sole

 4   member of unincorporated J&J and, thus, is personally liable for J&J’s breaches, as described

 5   below.

 6               b. Liévano Is Also Liable for Breaching Each Contract Identified in the

 7                   Complaint Because He Did Business as the Other Three Entity Defendants

 8            In addition to allegations against Liévano purely in his individual capacity, the Complaint

 9   raises allegations against him in his capacity doing business as the other three Entity Defendants:

10   Judang Team LLC, Perfeos LLC, and J&J. Specifically, the Complaint alleges that “Antonio Jose

11   Liévano (‘Liévano’), individually and acting through Judang Team, Perfeos, and his

12   unincorporated business Jot & Journeys (‘J&J’), (collectively, ‘Defendants’) operated a deceptive

13   and misleading advertising scheme on Facebook and Instagram.” Compl. ¶ 1 (emphasis added).

14   The Complaint describes multiple Facebook pages and Meta business and advertising accounts

15   created by and through Liévano for Judang Team, Perfeos, and J&J. Compl. ¶¶ 50-53. The

16   Complaint also directly links Liévano to the shell entities he created to orchestrate his scheme:

17   Liévano is the founder and sole member of Judang Team and Perfeos, and he operates J&J as an

18   unincorporated entity. Compl. ¶¶ 7-8. The facts alleged are sufficient facts to survive a motion to

19   dismiss and take discovery to prove that Liévano should be held liable for the actions of his

20   business entities.

21            The Defendants assert that no alter ego theory was pleaded to pierce the corporate veil

22   (e.g., no facts alleging commingling of assets or undercapitalization to treat Liévano as the entities’

23   alter ego). Mot. to Dismiss 5. To the contrary, Meta has alleged sufficient facts to infer, and expects

24   to prove through discovery, that Liévano should be held liable for the actions of his corporate

25   entities under an alter ego theory. “[W]hen the corporate form is used to perpetrate a fraud,

26   circumvent a statute, or accomplish some other wrongful or inequitable purpose, the courts will

27   ignore the corporate entity and deem the corporation’s acts to be those of the persons or

28   organizations actually controlling the corporation, in most instances the equitable owners.” Sonora
                                        5
         PLAINTIFF’S RESPONSE TO DEFENDANTS’ MOTION TO DISMISS COMPLAINT
              Case 3:25-cv-05156-TSH          Document 38         Filed 11/20/25      Page 6 of 15




 1   Diamond Corp. v. Superior Ct., 99 Cal. Rptr. 2d 824, 836 (Cal. Ct. App. 2000). “An individual

 2   can be deemed an alter ego of a corporation if: (1) there is a unity of interest and ownership such

 3   that the separate personalities of the corporation and the individual no longer exist, and (2) an

 4   inequitable result will follow if the acts are treated as those of the corporation alone.” Ultratech,

 5   Inc. v. Ensure NanoTech (Beijing), Inc., 108 F. Supp. 3d 816, 826 (N.D. Cal. 2015). Both are true

 6   here.

 7           In Ultratech, the court found that “[a]n officer may be liable for breach-of-contract if [the

 8   officer] was the alter ego of the breaching party.” Id. The court noted that the specific

 9   considerations necessary to prove an alter ego theory (e.g., commingling of funds, disregard of

10   corporate formalities, and undercapitalization) “are better evaluated with the benefit of discovery.”

11   Id. But at the pleading stage, the court found that plaintiff’s allegations in the complaint—“that

12   Wang was the president, principal, and sole owner of [the contracting company], that he controlled

13   all aspects of [the contracting company’s] business, and day-to-day operations, and that he

14   negotiated and signed the . . . agreement ”—were sufficient to infer that there was a unity of interest

 1             3. Meta’s Fraud Claim Is Not Barred by California’s Economic Loss Rule

 2             The Defendants erroneously argue that claims that their commission of fraud on Meta are

 3   barred because their actions occurred in the context of the contracts at issue here. Mot. to Dismiss

 4   at 7-8. Not so. In Robinson Helicopter Co. v. Dana Corp., 102 P.3d 268 (2004), the California

 5   Supreme Court held that the economic loss rule does not bar a plaintiff’s fraud and intentional

 6   misrepresentation claims when they are part of the inducement into the contract and are thus

 7   independent of the defendant’s breach of contract. That is the context in which the Defendants’

 8   fraudulent conduct occurred.

 9             The Robinson court explained that “[t]he economic loss rule requires a purchaser to recover

10   in contract for purely economic loss due to disappointed expectations, unless he can demonstrate

11   harm above and beyond a broken contractual promise.” Id. at 272. In allowing the plaintiff to

12   recover on both the breach of contract claim and the fraudulent intentional misrepresentation

13   claim, the court emphasized that tort damages are permitted in contract cases where one party

14   commits fraud during the course of entering into the contract. Id. at 273-275. The court explained

15   that “California’s public policy also strongly favors this holding,” noting that there is an “extra

16   measure of blameworthiness inhering in fraud” and “a contract is not a license allowing one party

17   to cheat or defraud another.” Id. at 275 (first quoting Lazar v. Superior Ct., 909 P.2d 981, 990

18   (Cal. 1996); then quoting Grynberg v. Citation Oil & Gas Corp., 573 N.W.2d 493, 501 (S.D.

19   1997)).

20             The Defendants here, like the defendant in Robinson, argue that the “fraud and

21   misrepresentation claims are not independent of the contract but are simply part of the alleged

22   breach of contract.” Robinson at 275; Mot. to Dismiss at 8. But as the Robinson court explained,

23   such an interpretation of the economic loss rule would “encourage[e] fraudulent conduct at the

24   expense of an innocent party.” Id. at 276.

26   Defendants, is inapposite.2 In UMG Recordings, the court noted that “[t]he rationale for the
